narration.whiteStork: The white stork is one of Europe’s most iconic and recognizable birds.
narration.migrationDistance: Each year, many migrate across vast distances between their breeding and wintering grounds.
narration.journeysChange: But these journeys do not always stay the same.
narration.environmentalQuestion: Together, we will explore how they have changed over time and what changing environmental conditions might have to do with it.
narration.realData: This story follows real routes of real white storks, using GPS tracking and environmental data.
narration.embodiedStory: Instead of only watching the data, you will experience it through your own body, using simple, dance-like movements to follow and represent the journey.

entry.title: Migration Change over Time
entry.subtitle: Compare five real migration cycles
entry.description: Follow how routes, timing, and wintering areas change from 2013 to 2023.

part1.title: Migration Change Over Time
part1.text: You know the migration cycle now. This time, we'll follow five real journeys from 2013 to 2023 without tutorial pauses.

part2.title: What to Notice
part2.text: Notice when each phase begins, how long it lasts, and where each stork spends the winter.

intro.title: 2013 to 2014
intro.text: We begin again with 2013 to 2014. This time, experience the cycle without the tutorial pauses.

autumnPrepare.title: Travel South
autumnPrepare.text: Get ready to travel south. This journey will take about {experienceDurationSecondsSpoken} seconds.

winterReflection1.title: Morocco
winterReflection1.text: You've reached Morocco. Remember how long that first journey south felt — it will be our reference for the cycles ahead.

springPrepare.title: Travel North
springPrepare.text: Get ready to travel north. The return journey will take about {experienceDurationSecondsSpoken} seconds.

breedingReflection1.title: Germany
breedingReflection1.text: Back in Germany on May 27. This completes our reference cycle.

summerTiming.title: Germany
summerTiming.text: For this reference cycle, simply notice how long the stork remains in Germany before leaving south.

winterTiming.title: Winter Timing
winterTiming.text: This long winter stay is part of the timing reference you'll compare with the later cycles.

autumnPrepare.title: Travel South
autumnPrepare.text: Get ready to travel south — about {experienceDurationSecondsSpoken} seconds this time.

winterReflection1.title: Morocco
winterReflection1.text: Back in Morocco — but the journey south was much shorter this time. It took less than three weeks.

springPrepare.title: Travel North
springPrepare.text: Now head north again — about {experienceDurationSecondsSpoken} seconds.

breedingReflection1.title: Germany
breedingReflection1.text: Back in Germany by March 26 — more than two months earlier than in our reference cycle.

summerTiming.title: Still in Germany
summerTiming.text: By this point, our reference stork had already left Germany. This stork is still here.

winterTiming.title: Winter Timing
winterTiming.text: By mid-September, the stork is already in its wintering area. In our reference cycle, it was still migrating south.

autumnPrepare.title: Travel South
autumnPrepare.text: Get ready to travel south — about {experienceDurationSecondsSpoken} seconds.

winterReflection1.title: Iberian Peninsula
winterReflection1.text: Something changed this time. The journey ended on the Iberian Peninsula instead of Morocco.

winterReflection2.title: Closer Wintering
winterReflection2.text: The stork is now wintering much closer to Germany.

springPrepare.title: Travel North
springPrepare.text: Time to head north — about {experienceDurationSecondsSpoken} seconds.

breedingReflection1.title: Germany
breedingReflection1.text: Back in Germany on March 13. The return has shifted earlier again.

summerTiming.title: Still in Germany
summerTiming.text: Again, we're past our reference departure point, and the stork is still in Germany.

winterTiming.title: Winter Timing
winterTiming.text: The winter stay begins at almost the same time as in 2016, but much farther north.

autumnPrepare.title: Travel South
autumnPrepare.text: Get ready — this journey south will be very short: about {experienceDurationSecondsSpoken} seconds.

winterReflection1.title: Short Autumn
winterReflection1.text: That was a remarkably short autumn migration — only six days in the tracking data.

winterReflection2.title: Iberian Peninsula
winterReflection2.text: Again, the stork spends the winter on the Iberian Peninsula.

springPrepare.title: Travel North
springPrepare.text: Get ready to return north — about {experienceDurationSecondsSpoken} seconds.

breedingReflection1.title: Germany
breedingReflection1.text: Back in Germany on February 23. Across this cycle, the two migrations together lasted only 22 days.

breedingReflection2.title: Reference Comparison
breedingReflection2.text: Compare that with the 129 migration days in our 2013 reference cycle.

summerTiming.title: Still in Germany
summerTiming.text: The previous two cycles had already started south by now. This stork is still in Germany.

winterTiming.title: Winter Timing
winterTiming.text: Despite leaving Germany later, the stork reached its wintering area by the same date as in 2018.

autumnPrepare.title: Travel South
autumnPrepare.text: Get ready to travel south — about {experienceDurationSecondsSpoken} seconds.

winterReflection1.title: Iberian Peninsula
winterReflection1.text: The autumn journey was a little longer again, but the stork still winters on the Iberian Peninsula.

breedingReflection1.title: Germany
breedingReflection1.text: Back in Germany on February 15. This spring migration began in January — the earliest of the five cycles.

breedingReflection2.title: Not Linear
breedingReflection2.text: The autumn journey became a little longer again, while the return shifted even earlier.

summerTiming.title: Still in Germany
summerTiming.text: We're even later in the year now, and the stork is still in Germany.

winterTiming.title: Winter Timing
winterTiming.text: This time, the winter stay begins later again, after the longer autumn journey.

structure.title: Five Journeys
structure.text: The annual cycle stayed recognizable, but its timing, duration, and destination changed across these five journeys.

pattern.title: Observed Pattern
pattern.text: Later examples included much shorter migrations, wintering closer to Germany, and substantially earlier returns.

qualification.title: Tracked Examples
qualification.text: The changes were not identical in every cycle, and these five tracked journeys are individual examples rather than a complete population trend.

question.title: Open Question
question.text: So what might be shaping these changing journeys?

climateTransition.title: Seasonal Environment
climateTransition.text: To broaden the picture, let's look at how the seasonal environment has changed over time.

entry.title: Climate Data
entry.subtitle: Changing Conditions
entry.description: Learn four seasonal movements, then use them to explore temperature change as context for white stork migration.

general.title: Movement Tutorial
general.intro: First, learn how each movement represents a value.
general.practice: You will practice the largest and smallest movement for each season.

summer.title: Circle radius
summer.explanation: Summer uses the radius of a circle. A larger circle represents a higher value.
summer.maximum: Draw the largest circle with fully extended arms.
summer.minimum: Draw a small circle close to your body.

autumn.title: Horizontal arc extent
autumn.explanation: Autumn uses the length of a horizontal sweep. A longer arc represents a higher value.
autumn.maximum: Sweep through the full horizontal semicircle.
autumn.minimum: Stop after a short horizontal arc.

winter.title: Body height
winter.explanation: Winter uses the height of your body. A smaller body represents a lower value.
winter.maximum: Stay fully upright for the maximum value.
winter.minimum: Crouch low and protect your head.

spring.title: Vertical blooming arc
spring.explanation: Spring uses the length of a vertical blooming arc. A longer upward arc represents a higher value.
spring.maximum: Complete the full arc above your head.
spring.minimum: Make a short, low blooming arc.

intro.title: Now use the movements to explore climate change over time.
intro.reference: We begin with the 1995-1999 reference period.

story.completionSubtitle: Winter and autumn show some of the largest later differences. Temperature provides context, not proof of what caused migration changes.

intro.context: We saw the storks' migration change over time. Now let's look at one possible environmental factor: temperature.
intro.encoding: Each season has its own movement, and one part of that movement represents the data value.
intro.scale: We scale the movements to the largest temperature difference in the data: 2.33 degrees. That is 100 percent; 50 percent represents about 1.17 degrees.
intro.range: First, you'll learn the largest and smallest version of each movement. For now, 100 percent simply means the full movement.
intro.watchThenMove: In the first bar, watch the avatar to remember the movement. Then perform the movement through the next three bars.

winter.encoding: First, winter. Your body height carries the value. At 100 percent, you stay at full height; lower values bring your body lower.
winter.maximum: Start with {value} percent: stay standing at your full height and follow the avatar.
winter.minimum: Great. Now the other end: at {value} percent, make yourself as small as you can and bring your arms over your head.
winter.complete: Well done. You now know the winter range.

spring.encoding: Next, spring. The arm arc carries the value. At 100 percent, complete the full arc above your head; at 50 percent, you would stop around shoulder height.
spring.maximum: Now start with {value} percent: complete the full arc until your hands meet above your head.
spring.minimum: Great. At {value} percent, follow the same arc, but raise your arms only a little.
spring.complete: Well done. You now know the spring range.

summer.encoding: Now, summer. The circle size carries the value. Start with your hands at your chest: at 100 percent, reach fully up and trace the largest circle; smaller values create a smaller circle.
summer.maximum: Now try {value} percent: reach fully up, keep your arms extended, and trace the largest circle.
summer.minimum: Great. At {value} percent, reach only a little and trace a very small circle.
summer.complete: Good. You now know both ends of the summer scale.

autumn.encoding: Finally, autumn. The sweep distance carries the value. At 100 percent, move all the way from one side to the other; at 50 percent, you would stop in front of your chest.
autumn.maximum: Now start with {value} percent: sweep all the way from one side to the other.
autumn.minimum: Great. At {value} percent, start from the same side but sweep only a quarter of the full distance.
autumn.complete: Great. You now know all four seasonal movement scales.

intro.chart: Now we'll move through 30 years of seasonal temperatures. The chart below fills in as you complete each movement.
intro.reference: We begin with 1995 to 1999, our reference period. For now, use the full movement for each season.

reference.winter: First, winter. Use the full movement to set our winter reference.
reference.spring: Now spring. Again, use the full movement to set the reference.
reference.summer: Next, summer. Use the full movement for our summer reference.
reference.autumn: Finally, autumn. Complete the full movement to finish our reference period.

referenceComplete.summary: Our reference is set. From now on, movement size shows how much each season differs from 1995 to 1999.
referenceComplete.scale: Remember: the full 100 percent movement represents the largest difference in the data.

2000_2004.winter: Winter: {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference — {movementValue} percent. Our first increase from the baseline.
2000_2004.spring: Spring is {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference. That's {movementValue} percent. A similar increase.
2000_2004.summer: Summer: {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference — {movementValue} percent. Close to spring.
2000_2004.autumn: Autumn is also {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference. That's {movementValue} percent.

2005_2009.winter: Winter: {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference — {movementValue} percent. Almost unchanged from before.
2005_2009.spring: Spring is {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference. That's {movementValue} percent. Again, little change.
2005_2009.summer: Summer: {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference — {movementValue} percent. Much closer to the baseline now.
2005_2009.autumn: Autumn reaches {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference — {movementValue} percent. A clear rise from before.

2010_2014.winter: Winter: {deltaAbsSpoken} degrees below the reference — minus 10 percent. This time, winter reverses direction.
2010_2014.spring: Spring is {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference. That's {movementValue} percent. Unlike winter, it stays above the baseline.
2010_2014.summer: Summer: {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference — {movementValue} percent. Still close to the baseline.
2010_2014.autumn: Autumn reaches {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference — {movementValue} percent.

2015_2019.winter: Winter: {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference — {movementValue} percent. A sharp rise from the previous period.
2015_2019.spring: Spring is {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference. That's {movementValue} percent. It rises as well.
2015_2019.summer: Summer: {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference — {movementValue} percent. A much larger difference than before.
2015_2019.autumn: Autumn reaches {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference — {movementValue} percent. Higher again.

2020_2024.winter: Winter: {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference — 100 percent. The largest difference in the dataset.
2020_2024.spring: Spring is {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference. That's {movementValue} percent. Slightly lower than before.
2020_2024.summer: Summer: {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference — {movementValue} percent. Almost unchanged.
2020_2024.autumn: Autumn reaches {deltaSpoken} degrees above the reference — {movementValue} percent. A strong final increase.

transition.2000_2004: All four seasons were above the reference. Next: 2005 to 2009.
transition.2005_2009: The seasons begin to diverge: summer moves closer to the baseline, while autumn rises. Next: 2010 to 2014.
transition.2010_2014: Winter fell below the reference, while the other seasons stayed above it. Next: 2015 to 2019.
transition.2015_2019: Now all four seasons have moved further above the reference. Next: 2020 to 2024.

completed.embodied: You have now moved through 30 years of seasonal temperature change.
completed.seasons: The seasons did not change equally. Winter and autumn end with some of the largest differences, while spring varies much less across the comparison periods.
completed.maximum: By the final period, winter is 2.3 degrees above our 1995 to 1999 reference — the largest difference in the dataset.
completed.maximumContext: That compares two five-year winter averages, making it a substantial shift in the seasonal conditions captured here.
completed.migration: Could changing temperatures be one factor shaping the storks' migration? These data cannot prove that connection, but they reveal part of the changing environment the storks migrate through.

entry.title: An Uncertain Future
entry.subtitle: Epilogue
entry.description: Bring the journey together and reflect on what may be shaping the changing migration of white storks.

narration.migrationRecap: Across these five journeys, migration changed in timing, duration, and winter destination.
narration.climateContext: Over recent decades, seasonal temperatures in Germany have changed as well.
narration.causalLimitation: But these data cannot show that climate alone caused any one stork to change its journey.
narration.otherInfluences: Food provided by humans, changed habitats, age, and migration experience may also shape the journey.
narration.finalReflection: Climate is one part of the changing environment, not the whole explanation. What will the stork's journey look like in the future?
